title: Heaps & Priority Queues
summary: Keeps the biggest (or smallest) thing always at your fingertips for O(log n) — the structure behind top-k, merge-k, Dijkstra, and streaming medians.

blocks.markdown:
A heap hands you the single most-extreme item cheaply, and lets you add more on the fly.

- A **priority queue** pulls out the highest-priority item next, not the oldest — like an ER treating the sickest first.
- A **binary heap** is the usual implementation: a **complete** tree (filled left-to-right, no gaps) obeying the heap property.
- **push** O(log n), **pop** O(log n), **peek** O(1), **build-heap** O(n).
- It gives you *one* extreme — not sorted order, not search by value. That narrowness is the point.

blocks.subTitle: When to reach for it
blocks.markdown:
Pick a heap when you repeatedly need the extreme of a changing set.

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Min or max, repeatedly, with inserts | Binary heap |
| Both min and max, or median | Two heaps |
| Full sorted order | Sort once |
| Search or range by value | Balanced BST |

blocks.subTitle: The heap property
blocks.markdown:
The heap property is the *only* ordering rule, and it keeps the extreme at the root.

- **Max-heap**: every parent ≥ both children, so the maximum sits at the root.
- **Min-heap**: every parent ≤ both children, so the minimum sits at the root.
- Siblings are **not** ordered relative to each other — the structure is only *partially* sorted.
- That loose ordering is exactly enough to keep the top item cheap and repairs local.

blocks.subTitle: Stored as a flat array
blocks.markdown:
A complete tree has no gaps, so it maps perfectly onto a plain array — no pointers needed.

```python
left_child(i)  = 2*i + 1
right_child(i) = 2*i + 2
parent(i)      = (i - 1) // 2
```

- The root is `H[0]`; reading the array left-to-right walks the tree level by level.
- A node at `i` is a leaf when `2*i + 1 >= size`.
- No per-node allocation means compact, cache-friendly memory.

blocks.subTitle: Sift-up (push)
blocks.markdown:
To push, drop the new value at the end and let it climb until the property holds.

```python
def push(H, value):
    H.append(value)
    i = len(H) - 1
    while i > 0 and H[i] > H[parent(i)]:
        swap(H, i, parent(i))
        i = parent(i)
```

- Appending at the end keeps the tree **complete**.
- At most one swap per level, log n levels → **O(log n)**, O(1) extra space.

blocks.subTitle: Sift-down (pop)
blocks.markdown:
To pop the max, take the root, move the last element up, and sink it back down.

```python
def sift_down(H, i, size):
    while True:
        largest, l, r = i, 2*i+1, 2*i+2
        if l < size and H[l] > H[largest]: largest = l
        if r < size and H[r] > H[largest]: largest = r
        if largest == i: break
        swap(H, i, largest); i = largest
```

- Always swap with the **larger** child — the smaller one would leave a bigger value below. **O(log n)**.

blocks.subTitle: Build-heap is O(n)
blocks.markdown:
Building a heap from n items at once costs **O(n)** — not O(n log n).

- Sift-down every non-leaf, from the last non-leaf back to the root.
- Most nodes are near the bottom and barely move: half are leaves (zero work), a quarter move one step, an eighth two steps.
- The sum `Σ h·n/2^(h+1)` converges to a constant times n.
- So **build in bulk** when you have all the data up front, rather than pushing one at a time.

blocks.subTitle: Heap vs BST vs sorting
blocks.markdown:
A heap is laser-focused on one extreme; other structures trade differently.

| Goal | Use |
|---|---|
| Repeated min/max, set changing | Heap |
| Search, range, k-th by value | Balanced BST |
| Full sorted output | Sort |

- Searching a heap for an arbitrary value is **O(n)** — it isn't a search tree.
- See [a08-trees-bst](a08-trees-bst.md) and [a17-sorting-selection](a17-sorting-selection.md).

blocks.subTitle: Decision rules
blocks.markdown:
Match the pattern to the structure.

- **Top k** of a large stream → a size-k heap, **O(n log k)** time, O(k) memory — not a heap of everything.
- **Both ends or median** → two heaps: a max-heap for the low half, a min-heap for the high half.
- **Merge many sorted sources** → a heap holding one frontier element per source.
- **One-shot in-place sort** → heapsort, O(n log n), O(1) extra space.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
Heaps are an internal building block in the systems you use daily.

- **Dijkstra** — a min-priority-queue picks the closest unvisited node; see [a12-graphs-shortest-paths-mst](a12-graphs-shortest-paths-mst.md).
- **Schedulers & event loops** — timers live in a min-heap keyed by fire time, so the soonest deadline is O(1).
- **Log/SSTable merges** — k-way merge keeps the smallest key from each input run.
- **Std libs** — Java `PriorityQueue`, Python `heapq`, C++ `priority_queue` are all just array + index math.

blocks.subTitle: Lazy deletion & signals
blocks.markdown:
In-place decrease-key is fiddly, so production code often uses **lazy deletion**.

- On a better path, push a fresh `(new_dist, node)` entry; skip **stale** entries when popped.
- Simple to code, costs only a few extra entries.
- Watch the **stale-entry ratio**: a high one means the heap is bloated and may need real decrease-key.
- Watch **queue depth** (producers outpacing consumers) and **bounded-heap size** (a missing `if size > k: pop` guard lets it grow).

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"A heap is sorted."** Only parent-child is ordered; the array is *not* sorted — reading it gives no order beyond the root.
- **"A heap is a BST."** Different rules; searching a heap for a value is O(n).
- **Wrong child on sift-down.** Swap with the *larger* child (max-heap), or you corrupt the property.
- **Breaking completeness.** Forget to move the last element into the root and the index math breaks.
- **One heap for the median.** A median needs both halves — that's the two-heap pattern.

blocks.subTitle: Stability & ties
blocks.markdown:
Heaps are **not stable** — equal-priority items can come out in any order.

- If equal priorities must come out **FIFO**, add a monotonically increasing sequence number as a secondary key.
- The tie then breaks by arrival order instead of arbitrarily.
- The same trick keeps comparisons well-defined when priorities collide and the payload isn't comparable.
